newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Key facts about Ireland's June 6 election.
newsitem.headline: Key facts about Ireland's June 6 election.

text.p: Ireland votes on Friday in elections to return a new parliament for a five-year term.
Following are key facts about the election, the main parties contesting them and their leaders:
There are 2,707,498 registered voters and 41 constituencies which will return 166 members of the Dail or parliament. Voting starts at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Friday and polls close 14 hours later.
The method of voting is proportional representation, allowing voters to list their candidates in order of preference.
The count will start at 9.a.m. (0800 GMT) on Saturday.

At the end of the first count any candidate who has received a number of votes equal to an agreed quota is elected; surplus votes are then transferred proportionally to the remaining candidates and counting continues until the fixed number of seats are filled for each constituency.

Ireland has been governed by coalitions for decades. But no sitting government has been returned for almost 30 years and most of the major parties have been in government with and in opposition to each other.
Major players are:
GOVERNMENT COALITION

FINE GAEL (47 seats) - Led by John Bruton. Came to power when previous coalition of Fianna Fail and Labour collapsed in late 1994. Sees itself as a progressive Christian Democrat party committed to reform. Bruton says it has balanced approach to quest for Northern Ireland settlement between pro-British Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists. Often portrayed as party of big farmers out of touch with the poor, a claim Bruton vigorously contests.

LABOUR PARTY (32 seats) Led by Dick Spring, the deputy prime minister and foreign minister. A left-leaning party which held balance of power in last two coalitions; its switch to partner Fine Gael led to allegations of being power-hungry. Reported to be declining in popularity in opinion polls, especially in key Dublin seats. Sees itself as champion of the workers and less advantaged in a booming economy.

DEMOCRATIC LEFT (6 seats) Led by Proinsias de Rossa. Formed from former members of Workers' Party. Sees itself as the voice of the dispossessed and least well off. Its agreement to Bruton's programme for government allowed it its first taste of power with de Rossa as social welfare minister. Accused by Fianna Fail of being responsible for high government spending because of its commitment to welfare programmes.
OPPOSITION PARTIES

FIANNA FAIL (68 seats) Led by Bertie Ahern, finance minister in previous Fianna Fail government. Centre-right, rarely out of power in past seven decades. Has adopted a get-tough-on-crime image for current election. Casts itself as the Irish republican party that would take a more assertive attitude with Britain in quest for Northern Ireland settlement. Says it is the party which looks after small farmers and business and has pledged to bring down the top 48 percent tax rate to 43 in five years.

PROGRESSIVE DEMOCRATS (8 seats) Led by Mary Harney, who is tipped for post of foreign minister if current coalition loses. Right of centre, zero-tolerance to drug issues, would drastically cut taxes, wants an overhaul of bloated state sector and would scrap unemployment benefit and replace with training allowance. Called for 25,000 redundancies in the civil service but backtracked after pressure from coalition ally Ahern. The party broke away from Fianna Fail in the 1980s. It has voiced doubts about joining EMU before Britain does.
OTHERS

SINN FEIN - (No seats) Led by Gerry Adams. Political wing of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fighting British rule of Northern Ireland. Says it is the only all-Ireland political party. Minimal electoral support (between two and four percent of votes) in European and national elections. Anti-EMU because this would surrender Irish sovereignty. May win one seat in the border Monaghan/Cavan area with Caoimhghin O Caolain.
GREENS - (1 seat) Led by Patricia McKenna, vigorously pro-environment. Wants a referendum on EMU. Fielding 26 candidates and may be a party to court in the event of a hung parliament.
IRELAND'S ECONOMY

One of the fastest growing and most robust in Europe. A combination of hi-tech foreign investment with agriculture and tourism, a mix that has created more than 1,000 jobs a week in the past two years. Solidly supported by EU grants to modernise its infrastructure to compete with the rest of Europe.
Irish real Gross National Product (GNP) grew at 6.5 percent in 1996 and is forecast to grow 5.75 percent in 1997.
Inflation, measured by the Consumer Price Index, was 1.5 percent between February 1996 and February 1997 (no figure avaliable for year 1996) and is forecast to be 1.8 percent in 1997.
The unemployment rate was 12.25 percent in 1996 and is forecast at 11.5 percent in 1997.
(Source for figures -- Central Bank of Ireland)
